lessons.text: Use position-based role labels ('your teammate at the back post') instead of jersey-color references — color cues are ambiguous without a diagram and aren't natural game-speak.
Cap scene complexity to 2–3 decision-driving cues per difficulty tier; each extra element beyond that raises working-memory load without improving the question.
Ensure each wrong answer requires a distinct reason to eliminate — no two distractors should share the same root flaw or be dismissible with a single inference.
Each distractor should test a different misconception or gap in game-sense, forcing the student to apply separate reasoning to rule it out.

Ensure every distractor is clearly wrong by targeting a different failure mode (e.g., wrong timing, wrong location, wrong action) — never let two options describe the same correct behavior at different levels of completeness.

When the stem asks for 'best approach,' make the test axis explicit in the stem (e.g., 'which describes complete pre-receive scanning') so the distinction between options cannot be argued on a dimension you aren't testing.
Always address the most tempting wrong answer explicitly in the explanation — if a distractor reflects a legitimate coached habit, state directly why it fails in this specific situation.
Ensure every factual claim in the explanation matches the scenario setup — never describe a game state (e.g., goalie out of position) that contradicts conditions already established in the question.
Verify every distractor dismissal against the scenario's own setup — if a player, puck, or position described in the stem contradicts your dismissal reasoning, fix the reasoning before publishing.

When the scenario includes a body-language or gaze cue, the explain must explicitly resolve it — name whether it is a misdirect or the dominant read signal, and state why, so the reasoning chain teaches the concept rather than just announcing the correct answer.

Ensure every distractor represents a distinct wrong instinct — never include two options that differ only in degree or timing of the same correct principle; each wrong answer must target a separate misconception.

Before finalizing the correct answer, stress-test it against every other option: if a well-coached player can defend a distractor with equal validity, add a scenario constraint that explicitly eliminates that distractor, or replace the distractor entirely.
When a plausible wrong answer shares a premise with the correct answer, the explanation must explicitly show why the wrong choice fails — not just why the right choice works.
Keep working-memory load manageable: limit simultaneous actor movements to the 2–3 that directly drive the decision, and reduce peripheral actors to a single static beat.

When writing answer options, ensure the correct answer is clearly superior by specifying the situational detail that makes alternatives inferior — never leave two options that are both tactically defensible under a plausible reading of the scenario.

Never pre-describe the scan result in the stem; present the situation before the read is made and let the player demonstrate they know what to look for, not just confirm a picture you already handed them.
Never give the correct answer narrative prominence in the stem — describe all options' targets with equal weight so no single actor or action is spotlighted.
Make the correct answer identifiable only through tactical reasoning, not through pattern-matching the most recently mentioned actor or detail in the setup.

Anchor every scenario with explicit positional context (who has the puck, where each defender is, who has slot coverage) so that exactly one answer is correct and all distractors are structurally wrong — not wrong by assumption.
Make the student recognize the developing threat from raw context clues (body angle, player movement); never hand them the cue directly and ask what to do next.

When the concept being tested is a *process or habit* (e.g., scanning, communication), the stem must force the student to demonstrate that process — not hand them pre-loaded scan data and ask them to execute. If the student can answer correctly without applying the concept, the question is testing something else.

Ensure every spatial reference in a scenario is unambiguous from the student's perspective: name the side (left/right from the player's POV), confirm the action is physically possible from the described position, and make the correct option's geometric advantage self-evident without relying on the explanation to rescue it.
Avoid using concept-title keywords in answer options — rephrase using hockey actions and outcomes so players can't pattern-match to the right answer without understanding the play.
Ground every answer's critique in facts established in the stem — if the stem doesn't specify position, angle, or numbers, don't use those as the reason a distractor is wrong.

Ensure exactly one option is clearly correct by giving every distractor a crisp, observable flaw — if two options require coaching-debate reasoning to separate, redesign the scenario so the inferior option has an unambiguous disqualifier (e.g., a closing defender, back to goal, no shooting lane).

Write the explanation around the single decision-making principle being tested, not a full adjudication of every option — if the explanation concedes an option is 'genuinely tempting,' treat that as a signal to fix the scenario, not the wording.
Never let a distractor option repeat or directly echo a constraint already stated in the stem — each wrong answer must be eliminable only through hockey reasoning, not by re-reading the setup.
Write all distractors before writing the stem, then audit the stem to ensure it contains no language that explicitly rules out any distractor.
Make every distractor a plausible action a real player might choose in that situation — eliminate any option a test-taker would immediately dismiss as absurd or irrelevant to hockey.
Keep each question anchored to exactly one concept: every option, including distractors, must be about that concept only — do not let distractors drift into a second skill or decision type.

Name the open space explicitly in the scenario setup — never make players infer geometry; if the read depends on a lane or zone being open, state it directly (e.g., 'leaving the front of the net unguarded').
Each answer option must affirm exactly one decision — strip downstream outcomes and compound clauses so the player is choosing a read, not a chain of events.
Write stems that present cues requiring interpretation — never pre-confirm the threat or pre-eliminate distractors in the setup text.
Set the scene one beat before the key action unfolds so students must anticipate what is about to happen, not react to what is already stated.
When a distractor describes real hockey advice, reword it to highlight why it is inferior — or explicitly rebut it in the feedback — so a well-coached player is never penalized for a defensible pick.
Feedback must address every tempting wrong answer, not just reinforce the correct one; close the loop on the most common wrong instincts.

When a distractor mirrors a real coaching principle, the setup must make that principle's failure condition visible — add a concrete timing or positioning detail that shows why it breaks down in this specific situation, not just in the explanation.

Write situation text so every answer option's correctness or incorrectness can be inferred directly from the setup; never rely on the explanation to supply facts (lane blocked, teammate's position, timing) that readers need to evaluate the choices.

Set up cues at the earliest recognizable stage of a pattern — an opponent's body angle or first stride — not after the threat is already obvious; the question must force anticipation, not confirmation.

Make every wrong answer a plausible alternative read a real player might choose (e.g., 'I have time to look for a longer pass'); never use distractors that violate basic physics or that any non-hockey player would instantly eliminate.
